body: The sanctuary cares for more than 100 rescued horses, ponies and donkeys, and feeding them is now one of its biggest running costs. It gets through about nine large bales of hay every week, and hay costs it around £5,400 a month.

courts.headline: Harlow hospital gets coroner warning over resuscitation decisions
courts.summary: A coroner's report says staff at the Princess Alexandra Hospital do not fully understand the rules on do not resuscitate decisions. The hospital has replied, setting out the changes it is making.
body: An Essex coroner has written to the Princess Alexandra Hospital in Harlow with concerns about decisions on resuscitation and mental capacity. Assistant coroner Stephen Simblet issued a prevention of future deaths report after the death of Luciana Gianfrancesco, 52, at the hospital. It went to the hospital trust and to Essex Partnership University NHS Foundation Trust (EPUT), which provided her mental health care. The report is dated 2 July 2026 and was published by the Courts and Tribunals Judiciary on 12 November.

The report says she died after being admitted with pneumonia and other health problems. It says doctors decided in April 2024 that she had capacity to refuse treatment. Her family and supported living staff disagreed. The report says this led to some delays in life-saving treatment, which she later agreed to have. It also says a do not resuscitate form was partly filled in by one doctor. Neither her family nor the consultant in charge knew about it, and no senior doctor signed it off.

The coroner raised three concerns. Staff are unsure how to assess capacity when a patient does not always accept life-saving treatment, and how to get advice from psychiatric staff. Clinical staff do not fully understand or follow the steps for making, recording and sharing do not resuscitate decisions. And it is not clear whether the hospital's resuscitation policies meet national standards for patients who are clinically obese. The inquest has not finished. It was adjourned after most of the evidence was heard, while more evidence on resuscitation is gathered.

In its formal reply to the coroner, dated 18 August and published alongside the report, the trust accepts there were shortcomings in how the do not resuscitate decision was documented and recorded. Its own policy says such a form must be endorsed by the patient's consultant within 48 hours, and that did not happen. The trust's cardiac arrest review panel found the records did not show the reasoning behind the decision or how the benefits and burdens of resuscitation had been weighed, and that the decision was not formally reviewed when one of the reasons for it, a high potassium level, improved.

The letter, signed by the trust's chief executive, chief medical officer and interim chief nursing officer, says a digital system for recording resuscitation and treatment escalation decisions, known as ReSPECT, is now in use across the hospital. Staff have been told that obesity or any other single condition must never on its own justify a do not resuscitate decision, and that a mental health diagnosis does not by itself mean a patient lacks capacity. The trust plans more training on resuscitation decisions and the Mental Capacity Act, clearer guidance on when to ask for specialist mental health advice, and continued audits. The letter gives no dates for these steps and has no separate answer on the coroner's concern about resuscitation policies for clinically obese patients.
points: Trust accepts the form was not signed off by a consultant within 48 hours
Digital system for recording resuscitation decisions now in use
The inquest will resume once further evidence on resuscitation is in

body: Two men, aged 19 and 25, were arrested on suspicion of grievous bodily harm after a man in his 30s was seriously assaulted in Market Row, Saffron Walden, Essex Police said. Officers were called at about 1.40am on Sunday 15 November.

Police said the man was attacked by a number of people and suffered several facial injuries. He was taken to hospital, and his injuries are not thought to be life-threatening. The two men were arrested on the Sunday afternoon and taken into custody for questioning.

Officers want to hear from anyone who saw an altercation earlier on the Saturday evening inside the Nexus Lounge on Market Hill, which they believe may be linked. Anyone with information or footage can contact Essex Police online or on 101, quoting incident 81 of 15 November.

body: A passer-by dialled 999 at 9.36pm on Tuesday 17 November after spotting a narrowboat on fire on the River Lee near Dobbs Weir Road in Roydon. By the time Essex County Fire and Rescue Service crews arrived, the boat was fully alight.

About 20 firefighters, some of them on-call firefighters who live or work within five minutes of their stations, worked to put the fire out. The fire service said no one was aboard the boat at the time.
Crews left the scene at 12.43am on Wednesday 18 November, and the fire service says an investigation will be carried out to establish the cause.

body: More than 300 people went to Epping Forest District Council's Tourism and Hospitality Job Fair at the Civic Offices in Epping on Thursday 12 November, the council said on Wednesday 18 November. Visitors looking for work, a change of career, seasonal jobs or apprenticeships met employers face to face.

The council ran the fair with the Department for Work and Pensions. Exhibitors included Epping Forest District Museum, Princess Alexandra Hospital's catering service, Lee Valley Regional Park, the Royal Gunpowder Mills, Harlow College, Visit Essex and Delta Hotels by Marriott.

Councillor Holly Whitbread, the council's portfolio holder for economic development, said tourism and hospitality offer careers for people of all ages and backgrounds, and that the event helped bring businesses and jobseekers together.

body: Colchester City Council opened its consultation on the 2027/28 budget on Monday 16 November, asking residents where it should cut, spend more or work differently. It names rising costs, steady demand for services and the growing cost of supporting people facing homelessness as the main pressures.

Councillor William Sunnucks, portfolio holder for resources, said: "We need your views on where we can save money." The answers will shape priorities for services including bin collections, parks, leisure, housing and community safety. People can fill in the online survey or attend a Residents' Panel session at the Town Hall from 10am to noon on Tuesday 8 December, or from 7pm to 8.30pm on Thursday 10 December.
Cabinet looks at the first draft budget position on Wednesday 2 December, and the consultation closes at 9am on Monday 14 December. Full Council sets the final budget in February 2027.

body: Colchester United were beaten by Tranmere Rovers in League Two at Prenton Park, Birkenhead, on Saturday 21 November 2026, with the home side's winner coming in the 90th minute. It ends a short lift for Danny Cowley's side, who had beaten Gillingham 2-0 a week earlier for their first league win since the end of August.

Tranmere had the better of the opening stages and went ahead shortly before the half-hour mark, when Ince, back in Darrell Clarke's starting line-up, picked up a loose ball, drove forward and finished. Colchester were level just before the break as Raggett scored from a Jack Payne cross, and the sides went in at 1-1. Jones then won it for Tranmere in the final minute of normal time.

Colchester went into the game 21st in League Two, three points above the relegation zone, and stay on 15 points. They are back at the JobServe Community Stadium against York City on Saturday 28 November (3pm), go to Grimsby Town on Tuesday 1 December, then host Mansfield Town in the FA Cup second round on Saturday 5 December.

stories.headline: Shrimpers lose five-goal table-top thriller
stories.summary: Tyreece Simpson and debutant Rico Richards struck two minutes apart after the break, but the Shrimpers could not complete the comeback against the runaway leaders.
body: Southend United 2-3 Boreham Wood. The Shrimpers' comeback against the National League leaders fell one goal short in front of 9,985 fans at Roots Hall on Friday night.

The Shrimpers were 3-0 down by the 33rd minute, with a former Southend player among the scorers. Oliver Bainbridge finished inside the near post on 19 minutes and Ben Whitfield converted at the far post on 29, both set up by Regan Booty, before ex-Shrimper Zak Brunt slammed in from close range from Whitfield's pass.

Southend made three changes at half-time, sending on Maxwell McKnight, Tyreece Simpson and Anthony Hartigan for Leon Chambers-Parillon, Omari Patrick and Zavier Massiah-Edwards. Simpson headed in McKnight's cross on 65 minutes, and two minutes later Rico Richards, making his debut after coming on for Oliver Coker just before the hour, fired in off the far post from Promise Omochere's pass.

Roots Hall roared for an equaliser through the remaining 23 minutes and four minutes of added time, but it never came. Southend were shown six yellow cards, to Omochere, Daniel Cox, Ben Goodliffe, Simpson, Hartigan and Darren Oldaker.
Head coach Kieron Dyer was back in the dugout after a one-match touchline ban for a game shown live on DAZN.
Boreham Wood's 15th league win of the season stretched their unbeaten start to 18 matches and moved them 13 points clear at the top of the National League.

body: Luc Benkenstein has left Essex by mutual agreement and will join Durham as part of the deal, the club announced on Thursday 19 November.

The all-rounder arrived at Chelmsford in 2021 and made his debut that season in the One Day Cup, against Durham. He went on to play 80 times for Essex across all formats, and had signed a contract extension that ran until the end of the 2027 season.

His father, former South Africa international Dale Benkenstein, was appointed a batting consultant at Durham in March. Essex thanked Benkenstein for his efforts and commitment and wished him well for the future.

After the break the home attack rarely troubled teenage Billericay goalkeeper Khari Ranson, and late on Jephcott tracked back to stop Jamie Mauge from shooting.

body: Brentwood Town lost 3-0 at home to Ramsgate at the Brentwood Arena on Saturday 14 November 2026 in the Isthmian League Premier Division, while Stanway Rovers drew 0-0 at Lewes. The defeat leaves Brentwood nineteenth on 16 points, and Stanway sit twenty-first on nine.

Prall kept the margin down by stopping a Paxman penalty shortly before the hour.

The defeat leaves Aveley fifteenth in the table. Their next game is away at Hutton in the Essex Senior Cup on Wednesday 11 November, and they return to league action at Carshalton on Saturday 21 November.

stories.summary: Luke Coulson struck twice before half-time for the hosts at the Optima Stadium, and Hubbard's late goal was only a consolation for the Iron.
body: Braintree Town suffered a heavy 4-1 defeat away to Weston-super-Mare in the National League South on Saturday. The Iron were three goals down within eight minutes of the restart and could not find a way back.

Weston had a goal from Ollie Hulbert ruled out for offside before Luke Coulson opened the scoring from around 30 yards with a deflected effort on 33 minutes. Coulson then converted a penalty on the stroke of half-time after Will Jenkins Davies was tripped, Hulbert made it three on 53 minutes and Jenkins Davies added a fourth six minutes later.
Hubbard pulled a goal back for Braintree on 86 minutes, and Louis Britton dragged a late one-on-one chance over the bar for the home side. The game was watched by a crowd of 962.

body: Billericay Town came away from Dagenham & Redbridge with a 2-2 draw in the National League South on Saturday. Elliot Long scored both goals for Billericay, who had to dig in after the break to protect a share of the points.

body: Chelmsford City fought back from a goal down to beat Farnborough 2-1 in the National League South on Saturday. The Clarets trailed at half-time but scored twice after the break to take all three points in front of their home supporters.

Farnborough captain Max Ehmer opened the scoring on 34 minutes. Clarke levelled six minutes into the second half, finishing after a run and cross from Barham, and Barham then struck from the penalty spot on 70 minutes to put City in front.

It was an eventful afternoon for Odegah, who had an early header ruled out for offside and was later booked for simulation after going down in the box. City saw out the closing minutes to secure the win, watched by a crowd of 1,523.

body: It was 4.27am when crews were sent to the house, after the residents' smoke alarms went off and woke them, Essex County Fire and Rescue Service said. The fire had started in a log burner. Firefighters had it out by 5.51am.

Watch Manager Kris Mortimer, from Tollesbury Fire Station, said: "Incidents like this show why it's so important to have working smoke alarms at home. Thankfully, the smoke alarms went off and woke the residents up. If they didn't have them, it could have been a very different incident."

The fire service advises having at least one working smoke alarm on every floor of a home and testing it once a month. Anyone without working alarms can contact the service at essex-fire.gov.uk/book or on 0300 303 0088.

stories.headline: Dartford tunnel shut: 90-minute delays and eight miles of queues
stories.summary: The east tunnel into Thurrock from Kent is still closed after a damaged joint was found overnight, and National Highways says the hold-ups are getting worse. No reopening time has been given.
body: National Highways said shortly after 9am on Monday 23 November that the east tunnel at the Dartford Crossing remained closed because of an infrastructure defect. Drivers face delays of 90 minutes on the approach, and building, with eight miles of congestion, the agency's East region said in its third update of the morning. The A2 was jammed in both directions on the approach to the Darenth Interchange, and diversion routes are in place.

The east tunnel carries northbound traffic from Kent into Thurrock, so all drivers heading for Essex are being sent through the smaller west tunnel, which has a 4.8m height limit. Earlier, KentOnline reported queues back to junction 3 of the M25 at Swanley and along the London-bound A2 past Gravesend.

National Highways said the damage, an expansion joint just in front of the tunnel entrance, was found during planned overnight work that was due to finish at 5am. Specialist crews have been working on it since, but the tunnel is not yet safe to reopen and stays shut until further notice.

The west tunnel is also booked to close overnight, from 9pm to 5.30am, between Monday 23 and Thursday 26 November for planned maintenance, according to National Highways' Dartford Crossing works page. Drivers are being told to plan ahead, allow extra time or avoid the crossing if they can. The Seax will update this story when the east tunnel reopens.

stories.headline: Wickford derailment repairs to cost Network Rail £3.65m
stories.summary: The bill covers the repairs after a Greater Anglia train came off the rails south of Wickford during August's heatwave. Investigators are still working out why it happened.
body: Network Rail has put the cost of repairing the line south of Wickford at £3.65m, covering heavy machinery hire and track repairs, as first reported by New Civil Engineer and Railnews. Together with £5.4m for the derailment at Lewes in East Sussex the day before, it leaves Network Rail facing a bill of about £9m from two derailments in two days last summer.

The Seax has gone back over the official record of what happened on Friday 14 August. The Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) says the train, running from Southend Victoria to London Liverpool Street, left the track at about 2.08pm, around 2.1 miles south-east of Wickford station near Salcott Crescent. Its data recorder shows it was doing about 77mph. The driver had seen a kink in the track that rocked the cab and was reporting it when they braked, after an emergency call from a train coming the other way.

The rear coach was dragged across the sleepers and ballast for about a mile and a half before the train stopped. It stayed upright. Ambulance crews, backed by two air ambulances, checked all 62 people on board and nobody needed hospital. Rayleigh and Wickford MP Mark Francois said the coach acted like a "knife" on the line: about 3,700 sleepers had to be replaced, along with signals and overhead power lines.

The line between Billericay and Hockley stayed shut for 12 days. Passengers took a shuttle train from Shenfield to Billericay, then buses to Wickford, Rayleigh and Hockley. Trains to Southend Victoria ran normally again from Wednesday 26 August, while the Southminster branch stayed on buses until 28 August for planned track renewals.

The cause has not yet been established. The RAIB, which opened a full investigation on 28 August, is looking at how the track was maintained, what was done to protect it in hot weather and how it was managed, and will publish a final report when its work ends. Network Rail has said the extreme heat and drought caused exceptional problems for the railway, and dried-out clay led to slower timetables on the Southend Victoria line from 1 September. Jamie Burles, managing director of GBR Anglia, said the operator was sorry for the disruption and thankful no one was hurt.

stories.summary: A four-year-old cat from Braintree got on an evening Greater Anglia train by himself and was only stopped when station staff in London spotted him.
body: Zeus, a half-British shorthair, boarded the 8.08pm service from Braintree on Tuesday 10 November, the BBC reports. Staff at Liverpool Street took him to their office, and Greater Anglia staff then travelled back to Braintree with him. Zeus wears two trackers and used to wander from the family's old home in Stansted Mountfitchet to London Stansted Airport.

body: The biggest moment comes at 10am on Tuesday 24 November, when a public inquiry opens at County Hall, Chelmsford, into the compulsory purchase and side roads orders for the £81m [Army and Navy roundabout scheme](/story/chelmsford-army-and-navy-public-inquiry-compulsory-purchase-24-november/). On the same day London Stansted holds a full-scale [emergency exercise](/story/stansted-airport-emergency-exercise-400-24-november/) with about 400 people from the airport and the county's emergency services. More emergency vehicles than usual will be seen near the airport.

Council business fills the rest of the week. Colchester's Local Plan Committee decides on Monday 23 November whether to recommend sending the [draft plan to the Planning Inspectorate](/story/colchester-local-plan-1800-responses-inspector-submission/) after 1,800 responses. Thurrock Council's Corporate Scrutiny Committee discusses [£27.3m of proposed savings](/story/thurrock-council-27-3m-savings-two-years-72-posts/) on Tuesday 24 November. That evening Basildon Council's Regeneration Scrutiny Committee looks at [£150,000 for town centre safety wardens](/story/basildon-town-centre-community-safety-wardens-150000-s106/), underpass cleaning and lighting. Maldon District Council opens a four-week consultation on the scope of its new Local Plan on Wednesday 25 November. On Thursday 26 November Basildon's cabinet decides on a [rent policy](/story/basildon-council-rent-convergence-extra-1-a-week-april-2027/) adding up to £1 a week for most council tenants from April 2027.

Christmas arrives in earnest on Thursday 26 November. Billericay's Late Night Light Up brings the town's first official lights switch-on since before the pandemic at 5.30pm, and Grays switches on its tree lights from 4.30pm. Light Up Leigh-on-Sea follows from 4pm on Friday 27 November, the day Cinderella opens at Chelmsford Theatre. B&M opens its first [Colchester city centre store](/story/colchester-b-and-m-st-johns-walk-former-wilko-opening/) at St John's Walk on Saturday 28 November, and Mind in West Essex holds its [Merry Minds Festive Fun Run](/story/harlow-merry-minds-festive-fun-run-water-gardens-mind-west-essex/) at Harlow's Water Gardens on Sunday 29 November. Full bids for UK Town of Culture 2028 are due on Monday 30 November, with [Basildon one of 15 towns shortlisted](/story/c-basildon-town-of-culture-phil-redmond-visit/).

stories.summary: Across Essex, the coming days bring a public inquiry into Chelmsford's biggest road scheme, council votes on savings and rents, and a run of Christmas lights switch-ons.

Staff from individual banks also see their own customers in private on set days: NatWest on Mondays, Barclays on Tuesdays, Lloyds, Halifax and Bank of Scotland on Wednesdays and Thursdays, and Santander on Fridays. Halstead Town Council announced on 12 August 2025 that the temporary hub was open at the church, behind the library. Cash Access UK thanked the church team for hosting it while a permanent home was found.

Cash Access UK chief executive Gareth Oakley said banking and payment habits were changing, which is why it is opening hubs and deposit machines that let small firms bank their cash. LINK, the UK's cash machine network, recommended a hub for Halstead after a request from the community. Six hubs are now open in Essex, with the others in Billericay, Hadleigh, Maldon, Rochford and Saffron Walden.

body: A fundraiser is gathering Pokémon cards, booster packs, tins, figures and toys for children who will spend Christmas on Phoenix Ward, the children's ward at Broomfield Hospital. Organiser Harry Fusedale is also raising money online to buy brand-new, sealed Pokémon products and unused toys for the ward's young patients, and says he has been in contact with the ward so that everything donated reaches the children.

Harry says Pokémon products can be hard to come by, and that opening a pack or finding a favourite character can mean the world to a child stuck in a hospital bed over the festive period. His aim is to bring "a little Christmas magic" to children and families who will be on the ward rather than at home.

Phoenix Ward, in the East Wing of Broomfield Hospital, gives specialised care to children and is run by Mid and South Essex NHS Foundation Trust. Harry is asking anyone with spare Pokémon items to get in touch, and anyone who cannot give to share the appeal. Donations can be made through Harry's GoFundMe site and there's a clickable link at the bottom of this page.

body: Ben Dobinson, 27, from Benfleet, spent more than 300 hours building a full-size, working Dalek for his modelmaking degree at the University for the Creative Arts in Farnham, Surrey, BBC News reports.

In his final-year show, he says he set himself the brief of a production company such as the BBC commissioning an accurate replica prop for a new production. It is based on the design used when Doctor Who returned in 2005. The university supplied tools and much of the wooden casing, and he spent up to £400 of his own money. When it was finished he spent about an hour driving it around the campus from inside.

Its main weakness, he told the BBC, is uneven ground, which can stop it in its tracks. The Dalek was designed by Raymond Cusick for the BBC in 1963, and fan-built replicas have long been a pastime in sheds and garages across Britain.

body: The Havens Hospices charity shop at the Stock Road recycling centre in Southend has sold 100 tonnes of pre-loved goods, Your Thurrock reports. The charity says the money raised pays for more than 4,000 hours of care at Little Havens Children's Hospice in Thundersley or Fair Havens Adult Hospice in Prittlewell.

The shop opened in May 2025 as a partnership between the charity, Southend-on-Sea City Council and SUEZ, which runs the city's recycling centres; it was the 34th reuse shop in SUEZ's network. In its first year its sales paid for 1,750 hours of specialist hospice care, and the council has since marked its 10,000th sale.

People can donate furniture, electrical items, televisions, glassware, crockery and bric-a-brac as they leave the tip, or buy them, at Stock Road, SS2 5QF. Some items, including child car seats, motorcycle helmets, stair gates and upholstered furniture without a fire safety label, cannot be taken. The charity is looking for volunteers on Wednesdays, Saturdays and Sundays.

body: Essex Highways has published its latest structural load assessment of Boxted Bridge, the 1897 crossing of the River Stour on Wick Road between Boxted and Suffolk, as pressure grows to settle its future. The county council says drivers must stay off it until the assessment of how much weight it can carry is complete, because it has no evidence yet that the bridge could safely take vehicles again.

The bridge was shut to everyone in an emergency closure on 30 June 2023, after an inspection found corrosion, cracking and deformation that had first been recorded in 2018. A load test in September 2025 found that a two-metre path through the centre could safely reopen to people on foot and on bikes, and the council consulted on that in January and February 2026. Its preferred long-term answer has been to replace the bridge, a plan its planning committee deferred in April 2025.

Bernard Jenkin, MP for Harwich and North Essex, has told the East Anglian Daily Times that council members need to "get a grip" and wants more testing to see whether the old bridge can be kept, and residents say traffic is being pushed through nearby villages. Campaigners from the Save Our Bridge group raised £12,300 for an independent load test, which the council did not allow, and say a freedom of information request showed Essex Highways spent £756,640 on plans for the bridge between 2016 and December 2025. The council says it sent further technical reports to its planners in October.

body: Two professors at the University of Essex's Colchester campus at Wivenhoe Park are on Clarivate's Highly Cited Researchers 2026 list: the plant biologist Tracy Lawson and the psychologist Reinhard Pekrun. The list picks out scientists and social scientists whose papers rank in the top 1% by citations in their field over the past decade.

Clarivate named 6,802 researchers from more than 1,200 universities and institutes in 62 countries and regions this year. It says roughly one in every 1,000 of the world's scientists and social scientists makes the cut.
## Crops for a changing climate

Professor Lawson, from the School of Life Sciences, has been on the list for seven years in a row, the Daily Gazette reports. Her research looks at photosynthesis, at how the tiny pores on leaves open and close, and at how efficiently plants use water, with the aim of breeding crops that hold up better in drought and heat.

In August she won the International Society of Photosynthesis Research's Innovation Award for technology that has changed how scientists measure those processes. In 2024 she oversaw the opening of the £3m STEPS lab at Essex, where crops are grown in conditions set up to mimic a future climate.
## Why students feel what they feel

Professor Pekrun, from the Department of Psychology, studies how emotions such as enjoyment, anxiety and boredom affect students' motivation and results. He devised the control-value theory of achievement emotions and the Achievement Emotions Questionnaire, which researchers use to measure feelings such as test anxiety.

He first joined Professor Lawson on the list in 2024, when the university said he had published more than 350 books, articles and chapters. He told the Gazette this year's recognition was down to teamwork and the support of colleagues, students and staff at Essex.
stories.headline: Essex's Tracy Lawson and Reinhard Pekrun on world's most-cited list

body: The University of Essex is offering a fully funded three-year doctorate on Marianne Straub, one of the most influential British textile designers of the 20th century, who spent two decades designing for Warner & Sons in Braintree. The project, Fabric of Everyday Life: Marianne Straub, Textile Innovation and Design, 1950-1970, is a partnership with the Warner Textile Archive, which is owned by Braintree District Museum Trust.

The university says Straub's work remains underexamined by academics despite how widely it was used: on the London Underground, London buses, in airports, public buildings and homes. She set out to make well-designed, practical fabrics that ordinary people could afford.
## From Switzerland to Great Bardfield

Born in Amriswil, Switzerland, in 1909, Straub came to England in 1932 to study power-loom weaving in Bradford, because Swiss technical colleges did not then admit women. She advised 72 Welsh woollen mills in the 1930s, became head designer and later managing director of Helios, and joined Warner & Sons in 1950.

Her Surrey fabric, based on a crystal structure, was shown at the Festival of Britain in 1951, and she lived among the artists of Great Bardfield from 1953. Her blue and green moquette, known simply as Straub, was used on London Transport buses and trains from 1969, including the Piccadilly line extension to Heathrow. Her fabrics for Tamesa also went into the QE2 liner and BEA's Trident airliners. She taught at the Central School of Art, Hornsey and the Royal College of Art, was made a Royal Designer for Industry in 1972, and died in 1994.
## What the researcher will do

The student will be the first to work through the Marianne Straub Collection, which the archive is acquiring: 11 boxes including her personal diaries and her letters to leading figures in industrial design. They will catalogue it to a professional standard and combine it with Warner's own design books, samples and business records.

The post, funded through the Essex AHRC Doctoral Landscape Awards, pays a stipend of £21,805 a year plus tuition fees, with up to £9,000 for travel to the archive. The student will spend a day a week at the archive in Braintree and be based at the university's Colchester campus. It is open to UK and international applicants, with interviews planned for early March 2027.
The Warner Textile Archive is the largest publicly owned collection from a luxury textile manufacturer in the UK, and University of Essex students already research its designers on placements there.
stories.headline: Funded PhD to tell the story of Marianne Straub, Braintree's Tube seat designer
points: Applications close at midday on 10 February 2027

stories.summary: The University of Essex and Braintree's Warner Textile Archive want a researcher to explore the Swiss-born weaver whose fabrics covered London Underground seats and the QE2.

body: Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader and MP for North West Essex, visited Stansted Airport College on the afternoon of Friday 20 November to see how its students move from education and training into work, Your Harlow reports. Harlow Council leader Dan Swords and Harlow College principal Karen Spencer joined her as she toured the workshops, before she sat down with students for a roundtable.

The visit came in a week when young people not in education, employment or training, and the number of people out of work and not looking for a job, were in the news. Your Harlow says more than 15,000 Harlow residents are classed as economically inactive. Mrs Badenoch gave the site an interview on jobs, apprenticeships and welfare.

The college, at the end of Stansted's runway, opened in September 2018 as a partnership between London Stansted Airport and Harlow College, the first of its kind at a UK airport. It trains more than 500 young people a year in aviation engineering and other airport skills, and the airport, in Mrs Badenoch's constituency, has said its expansion plans would let the college take more students.

body: Southend-on-Sea City Council is facing growing calls to set a firm date for the pier's £3.5m electric trains to run again, the Yellow Advertiser reports.

body: Harlow Council has finished rebuilding Market Square from the ground up, the first phase of its plan to bring the heart of the town centre back to life, Your Harlow reports. The square now has a water jet feature at its centre, granite paving, planting and rain gardens, seating, new lighting and CCTV, with space set aside for market stalls and outdoor events.

A weekly market will return from February 2027, with independent traders selling fresh produce, artisan food and gifts. Work has moved on to the buildings around the square: the landmark clock on Adams House is being restored and its ground floor turned into an all-day food and drink venue with live entertainment and outdoor dining, Market House is becoming office space, and work is under way at The Rows.

The council appointed Hill Partnerships to carry out the rebuild, backed by £23.7m from the government's Towns Fund, and bought Market House and Adams House, putting the square's clock under local control for the first time in decades. Building started in October 2025 and was first due to finish in spring 2026. Council leader Dan Swords said the new square was built to the standard of the best town centres.

body: A public inquiry into Essex County Council's plans to buy land for the £81m Army and Navy scheme in Chelmsford opens at 10am on Tuesday 24 November on the fourth floor of County Hall, Chelmsford City Hub reports. A government-appointed inspector will hear objections to the council's compulsory purchase order and side roads order, then report to the Transport Secretary, who decides whether to confirm them.

The scheme would replace the roundabout with a "hamburger" roundabout, with a road running through its middle, alongside walking, cycling, bus and Park and Ride improvements. It won planning permission in November 2024, and the government confirmed it would go ahead after its spending review. When the council consulted, 60% of more than 840 people who replied chose the hamburger design.

The council published compulsory purchase orders in case it could not agree terms with landowners, and warned early on that objections could lead to an inquiry. Objections now cover land acquisition, environmental mitigation, speed limits, a business car park and land for expanding Sandon Park and Ride. Plans to expand the Chelmer Valley Park and Ride were dropped from the scheme this year to keep it within budget after construction costs rose.

body: Trains between Essex and London Liverpool Street will not run on seven weekend days in January and February 2027 while Network Rail carries out follow-up work on the Great Eastern Main Line, it announced on Tuesday 17 November. The cancellations, first reported by the Romford Recorder, hit Greater Anglia, the Elizabeth line and the Liberty line between Romford and Upminster.
## When trains will not run

On Saturday 9 and Saturday 16 January, Greater Anglia will run no trains between Ingatestone and Liverpool Street. Trains from Norwich, Ipswich and Clacton will terminate at Shenfield, with replacement buses from Ingatestone to Newbury Park for the Central line. Southend Victoria and Southminster trains will run only as far as Shenfield, with buses from there to Newbury Park.

Five Sundays are affected: 10, 17, 24 and 31 January and 14 February. Greater Anglia's main line services will start and finish at Beaulieu Park, north of Chelmsford, with a coach link onward. On the Southend line, trains will reach Billericay on the first two of those Sundays; on the other three, the whole route from Southend Victoria towards the capital is bus-only, as is the branch from Southminster to Wickford.

On all seven days there will be no Elizabeth line trains between Liverpool Street and Shenfield, and the Liberty line will not run. Replacement buses will run from Stratford to Romford, and passengers for Gidea Park, Harold Wood, Brentwood and Shenfield should change at Chadwell Heath. Greater Anglia tickets will be accepted on the Central line between Newbury Park and Stratford or Liverpool Street.
## What the work involves

Engineers will adjust six new sets of points at Forest Gate and two at Stratford, which are being installed during a 10-day closure from 27 December to 3 January, and refurbish points at Pudding Mill Lane and Shenfield. In Essex, rails will be renewed at Brentwood, Rayleigh and Hockley, overhead wires repaired between Romford and Chelmsford and between Wickford and Southminster, canopies repainted at Shenfield and repaired at Southminster and Hockley, and the footbridge at Wickford mended. Specialist trains will also clear leaves and clean the rails.

Martin Beable, chief operating officer of GBR Anglia, said the work was "very important to help maintain the safe and reliable running of the railway", and asked passengers to check before they travel and allow extra time. Greater Anglia lists the changes on its service alterations page, Elizabeth line and Liberty line passengers can use TfL's Journey Planner or the TfL Go app, and National Rail Enquiries has the latest advice.

stories.headline: The week in Essex: Brentwood School review, oysters and Three Shells
stories.summary: The ten stories that shaped the county this week, where each stands now, and the dates to watch in the week ahead.
body: It was a week of a damning school review, a decision on a Southend landmark and fresh hope for the county's oyster farmers. Here is where the main stories stand on Sunday evening, and what happens next.

[Brentwood School's independent safeguarding review](/story/brentwood-school-safeguarding-review-british-fencing-own-review/), published on Friday, found that Gareth Stafford Bull, the school's fencing coach from about 1982 until he was sacked in 1997, probably abused a number of boys. It also found the school let down former pupils who came forward after his death: in 2008 the headmaster of the day told one of them he had seen no evidence, although the school's own files recorded that police had found prima facie evidence against Bull in 1997. British Fencing is now setting up its own inquiry into what was known.

Oyster farmers on Mersea, the Colne, the Crouch and the Roach [could win back European buyers](/story/essex-oyster-farmers-eu-trade-uk-eu-deal-class-b/) under the food and farming deal the UK and the EU agreed in Brussels on Friday. Since 2021 the EU has refused shellfish from waters graded Class B unless it has been purified first, and a Seax analysis of the Food Standards Agency's list found that 27 of the 33 oyster zones on the Essex coast carry that grade all year round. The change is expected from March 2028.

On Monday Southend-on-Sea City Council's cabinet [backed an £800,000 plan to remove Three Shells Lagoon](/story/southend-three-shells-lagoon-cabinet-decision-day/) beside the pier and return the site to natural beach. The lagoon opened in July 2016 and has been fenced off for most of this year, after a mother and daughter had to be pulled out of waist-deep sand in March. Building, repairing and dismantling it will have cost about £2.84m.

On the Dengie Peninsula, Low Carbon's plan for [one of the UK's biggest solar farms](/story/dengie-peninsula-solar-farm-4200-acres-seven-sites/) would cover 4,200 acres across seven sites between Bradwell and Burnham-on-Crouch and could generate up to 1GW. Simon Morgan, leader of Maldon District Council, estimates it would take up almost a third of the peninsula's land. A wider public consultation is planned for early 2027, before the firm applies to the government for consent.

[Maldon Salt](/story/maldon-salt-council-no-concerns-trading-standards-labelling/) stayed in the spotlight after an Observer investigation found the firm mixes German rock salt into its sea salt. Maldon District Council says it has no concerns about the firm's sites. Labelling is a matter for Essex County Council's trading standards service, which looked at how the salt is made in 2019 and decided no further action was needed.

[A Seax analysis of police.uk data](/story/essex-recorded-crime-september-2026-police-data/) found police in Essex logged 2,042 reports of anti-social behaviour in September, up 76% on a year earlier, with rises in 50 of the force's 56 neighbourhood areas. Recorded crime rose more slowly, to 12,530 offences, while robbery fell 19%.

In Braintree district, the Home Office has [sent its plan to extend the Wethersfield asylum centre](/story/wethersfield-asylum-centre-home-office-urgent-crown-development-braintree/) straight to ministers through the Urgent Crown Development route, bypassing Braintree District Council. It wants the centre to stay open beyond April 2027 and to raise its capacity from 800 to 1,245 people. [A police dispersal order around the former airbase](/story/braintree-raf-wethersfield-dispersal-order-21-23-november/) runs until midnight on Monday.

Braintree's MP, [Sir James Cleverly, was chosen as the Conservative candidate for London mayor](/story/braintree-mp-james-cleverly-conservative-london-mayor-candidate/) at the election in May 2028, and opened his campaign by attacking Lord Khan's record on crime and housing. [BAE Systems, which has a base at Great Baddow](/story/bae-systems-1070-job-cuts-great-baddow/), announced plans for up to 1,070 UK job cuts, though it has not said whether staff in Chelmsford are affected.

Colchester lost a link to one of television's great satires. [Peter Fluck](/story/colchester-spitting-image-peter-fluck-dies-85/), the co-creator of Spitting Image, who taught at Colchester School of Art in the 1970s, died at his home in Cornwall on Saturday, aged 85.
## The week ahead

On Monday Colchester's Local Plan Committee [decides whether to recommend sending the city's draft plan to a government inspector](/story/colchester-local-plan-committee-23-november-preview/), after more than 1,800 responses to the final consultation. On Tuesday a government-appointed inspector opens [the public inquiry into the land deals for Chelmsford's £81m Army and Navy scheme](/story/chelmsford-army-and-navy-public-inquiry-compulsory-purchase-24-november/), at County Hall from 10am.

On Saturday B&M opens [its first Colchester city centre store](/story/colchester-b-and-m-st-johns-walk-former-wilko-opening/) in the former Wilko unit at St John's Walk, empty since October 2023. Looking further ahead, Colchester City Council's cabinet decides on Wednesday 2 December whether to [upgrade Leisure World rather than rebuild it](/story/colchester-leisure-world-rebuild-ruled-out-cabinet-2-december/).

body: Green bins across Rochford district will be emptied every other week from Monday 23 November in a four-month winter trial. Rochford District Council's Environment Committee approved the pilot on Thursday 1 October, and it ends on 29 March 2027, when weekly rounds return.

The council says the amount going into green bins has dropped sharply since separate weekly food waste collections began: about 7,000 tonnes were collected between November and July in the two years before, against about 3,000 tonnes in the same months since. Demand also falls every winter, peaking in May and bottoming out in February, while longer trips to disposal sites, more homes and rising costs squeeze the service. Councillor Tino Callaghan, who chairs the Environment Committee, said "this is a trial and not a permanent change".

Food waste caddies will still be emptied every week, and extra garden waste left beside bins will not be taken, so the council suggests home composting or a trip to Rayleigh Recycling Centre. There will be no council tax reduction, because councils are not legally required to collect garden waste at all. A district-wide consultation runs during the pilot, and councillors will weigh it alongside the trial results before deciding the service's future.

stories.headline: Clacton 8th in UK for signing petition to jail drivers who hide crashes
stories.summary: The petition wants mandatory prison for drivers who hide a crash or hold up a police investigation. Essex has under 3% of the UK's constituencies but about 7% of its signatures.
body: Drivers who knowingly avoid reporting a crash, even if they believed they had only hit an animal, would face a mandatory prison sentence under a petition to Parliament that is spreading fast in Essex.

The petition, started by Chloe Mefford, says some drivers stay silent so that alcohol or drug levels can fall below the legal limit, or to hide a victim. It also wants prison for drivers who pervert the course of justice or refuse to help an investigation, which it says causes great distress to families. It opened on 2 October and closes on 2 April 2027.

At present, failing to stop after a crash or to report it is dealt with by magistrates, with a maximum of six months in prison and an unlimited fine. Under sentencing guidelines, even the most serious cases start at a community order, with up to 26 weeks in custody possible.

By 5.33am on Sunday 22 November, 4,101 people in Essex had signed, out of 57,530 across the UK. Clacton has 537 signatures, eighth of all 650 constituencies and first in the county. Chelmsford (387), Maldon (386), Harlow (382) and Witham (330) come next. The fewest are in Thurrock (84), Southend West and Leigh (79) and Southend East and Rochford (69).

The petition passed 10,000 signatures on 27 October, so the government will publish a response. It had not done so by Sunday morning. If it reaches 100,000, Parliament will consider it for a debate. Signature counts show where a petition has been shared, not what everyone in an area thinks.

body: Oyster farmers and fishermen on Mersea, the Colne, the Crouch and the Roach could win back European customers they lost after Brexit, under the food and farming deal the UK and the EU agreed in Brussels on Friday.

Since 2021 the EU has refused live oysters, mussels, clams and cockles from British waters graded Class B unless they have already been purified. Class B waters are clean enough to farm shellfish but not clean enough for them to be eaten straight from the water. Before Brexit, shellfish from those waters was sent to the continent and purified there.
## Most Essex oyster waters are Class B

A Seax analysis of the Food Standards Agency's latest classification list, updated on 1 October 2026, shows how hard that rule hits the county. Of the 33 harvesting zones on the Essex coast graded for native or Pacific oysters, 27 are Class B all year round, one of which also closes every September. Two are Class A only in some months, and just four are Class A all year.

Six of the seven West Mersea oyster zones are Class B, including Ray Creek, Strood Channel and Salcott Channel. Little Ditch is the exception, graded Class A from November to April. Every oyster zone on the Colne, the Crouch and the Roach is Class B, as are the three in the Walton Backwaters. The Blackwater is mixed: Ray Channel, St Peter's Flats and St Peters & Batchelor are Class A all year, Outer Blackwater is Class A from September to April, and Central Blackwater, Goldhanger and Osea South are Class B.
Cockles tell a similar story. The cockle beds on Southend Flats, Maplin West and Maplin Central are Class B, while Maplin East and the Barrows are Class A only from June to September.
## What the deal changes
The government's guidance for fish and shellfish businesses says it expects the agreement to reopen exports of live shellfish from Class B waters to the EU for purification.

Seafish, the industry's public body, estimated that Britain's live shellfish trade with the EU was worth about £15 million in 2019, mostly mussels, oysters, cockles and clams. Essex's share has never been published. Seafish says the new agreement could cut costs and delays for seafood businesses trading with the EU.
The ban was felt quickly on Mersea. In 2021 one oysterman told ITV Anglia it had "devastated business".
## When it starts

Nothing changes yet. The government says the agreement will apply from 1 March 2028, subject to approval procedures on both sides, with transition arrangements in a few areas. Until then the current checks and paperwork stay.

When it applies, Britain will follow EU rules on food safety and animal and plant health. In return, most routine certificates, advance notices and border checks on food traded between Britain and the EU will go. The government says the deal could add up to £5.1 billion a year to the UK economy by 2040.
## Fishing and the Thames ports
The summit also confirmed full access for British and EU boats to each other's fishing waters until 30 June 2038.

For the Thames ports the picture is mixed. Food from the EU arriving at London Gateway, Tilbury and Purfleet should face fewer checks. But the National Farmers' Union says the UK's current system of prioritised checks will be dropped, which means a larger share of food arriving from outside the EU could be checked at the border.
## Centuries of Essex oysters

Oysters have been taken from the Colne since Roman times, and each autumn the Mayor of Colchester dredges the first native oyster of the season in the Pyefleet Channel. The Haward family has farmed oysters on Mersea since at least 1769.

Native oysters on the Blackwater, Crouch, Roach and Colne are now managed under a permit scheme run by the Kent & Essex Inshore Fisheries and Conservation Authority, because the four estuaries form a Marine Conservation Zone.

body: Peter Fluck, the artist and caricaturist who co-created the satirical television series Spitting Image, has died aged 85.
Fluck, who taught art at Colchester School of Art during the 1970s, died at his home in Cornwall in the early hours of Saturday, November 21, following a recent illness, his family said.

He became one of the most influential figures in British television satire through Spitting Image, the ITV programme which used grotesque puppet caricatures to mock politicians, celebrities, royalty and other prominent figures.
But before the show made him a household name, Fluck spent part of his career teaching aspiring artists in Colchester.
## From art teacher to television satire
Born in Cambridge in 1941, Fluck studied at Cambridge School of Art, where he met fellow artist Roger Law.
The pair went on to establish a creative partnership, initially working as freelance illustrators and caricaturists before developing the idea that would transform their careers.
Spitting Image first aired in 1984, bringing their exaggerated puppet creations to television screens across Britain.

The programme became famous for its uncompromising portrayal of the country's political establishment, with Margaret Thatcher, John Major, members of the Royal Family and international figures among its regular targets.
At its peak, the series attracted audiences of around 15 million viewers and became one of the defining television programmes of the 1980s and 1990s.
It ran for 18 series before ending in 1996.
## A lasting legacy
Fluck and Law's creations helped redefine political satire, combining caricature, puppetry and comedy to produce some of the most recognisable television characters of their era.
The programme won numerous awards, including two Emmy Awards, and its influence extended beyond television into music, popular culture and political commentary.
After Spitting Image ended, Fluck continued his artistic career, turning his attention to sculpture and moving installations from his studio in Cornwall.
His family described him as a private man who avoided fame and attention.
In a statement, they said: "The spirit that Spitting Image brought to the country was epoch defining.
"With Roger Law ('Luck and Flaw'), he brought a unique cutting edge to caricaturing that later evolved into a production company that created the TV series Spitting Image."
They added that his creative life continued for many years after the programme from his studio in Cornwall.
His death marks the loss of one of the artists behind a television phenomenon which remains synonymous with British satire.
stories.headline: Spitting Image co-creator Peter Fluck, who taught art in Colchester, dies at 85
stories.summary: The artist helped create one of Britain's most iconic television programmes, but before achieving worldwide fame he taught at Colchester School of Art.

body: Gareth Stafford Bull, Brentwood School's fencing coach from about 1982 until he was sacked in 1997, probably abused a number of boys at the school, an independent review commissioned by its governors has found. The review also says the school let down former pupils who came forward in the years after his death.

When one of them raised concerns with the school in 2008, the headmaster of the day replied that he had seen no evidence, even though the school's own files recorded that police had found prima facie evidence against Bull in 1997.

Bull was himself a Brentwood pupil before he returned as its fencing instructor. Published results show he fenced for the school as a boy, finishing third in the boys' senior sabre at the 1974 Public Schools' Fencing Championships. The review says he also coached the England under-20 fencing team, and that former pupils told it he abused other boys while he was still a pupil and went on doing so throughout his time as a coach.

He was suspended and then sacked for gross misconduct in April 1997, after police told the school that pupils had raised concerns about him. He died in May 1997 before the police investigation could go further, so he never faced trial. The review's findings about him are made on the balance of probability, the standard used in civil cases, rather than the criminal standard of beyond reasonable doubt.
## Who wrote the review

The findings come from the "Review into the abuse by David Pickthall of pupils and former pupils of Brentwood School", a 59-page report commissioned by the school's governing body and published on the school's website this month. It was led by two independent members. Louisa Spicer, who chaired it, is a former solicitor with more than 20 years' experience in employment law and human resources. Jane Foster (Sarre) is an independent safeguarding adviser, consultant and trainer who has led school safeguarding audits. They were supported by three governors who had no part in managing Pickthall: Bob McLintock, John Griffith-Jones and the Venerable Chris Burke. The Seax has read the full report.

The governors commissioned the review on 23 November 2024, days after Pickthall, the school's former director of music, was jailed. He admitted 29 offences against 19 male victims between 1979 and 2021, most of them his former pupils, and was sentenced to 12 years with a further four on extended licence. He was asked to take part in the review but declined. It began work in March 2025, and as well as Pickthall's abuse, its remit covered other historical allegations about former members of the school community. That is where the findings about the fencing coach appear.
The reviewers say the school kept virtually no records for the 1980s and 1990s, so they relied heavily on court transcripts and on accounts from former pupils and staff.
## What happened in 1997

The details of Bull's appointment are not in his personnel file, which is thin. Its first document is a complaint from the head of Brentwood Prep in May 1989 that he was unreliable and missed lessons. In 1990 the headmaster gave him a first written warning over his absences and an unpaid accommodation bill of £1,000, while praising his "tremendous success" as a coach and telling him the school was in his debt.

In April 1997 the headmaster wrote to the parents of pupils involved in fencing to tell them Bull had been suspended. A note on his file records that a small group of boys had come forward to a member of staff. The concerns included encouraging boys to shower after competitions and joining them. Governing body minutes from 21 April record that police enquiries, prompted by an anonymous call, had found prima facie evidence of indecent behaviour involving members of the school fencing team, particularly on trips away. By then Bull was missing from home, and the headmaster judged the evidence against him to be incontrovertible. He was dismissed the next day.

The headmaster gave police a list of pupils who had been taught by Bull, and officers interviewed them at the school. On 27 April more pupils who had contact with him were seen one by one in the headmaster's office. The brief notes kept from those meetings confirm that a number of pupils said Bull had suggested they shower with him. Bull died on 5 May 1997, and his death and the police investigation were reported in the national press.
## What former pupils told the review

One former pupil told the review that Bull abused boys on what he called "an industrial scale", including intimate massages, coming into boys' rooms on residential trips, sexualised conversation and invasive questions about their sexuality. Bull travelled alone with pupils and sometimes shared rooms with them. They said he also befriended parents, visiting their homes and having dinner with them. One described him as effectively part of the staff although he was not a full-time employee, coming and going as he pleased, and said pupils talked about him only on a surface level. Contributors said staff must have heard rumours. The review says the full extent of his offending is not known and that more victim-survivors may come forward.
## How the school handled later complaints

Former pupils contacted the school about Bull in 2008, 2017 and 2024. In 2008 a former fencer told the headmaster of the time, who had not been at the school while Bull worked there, that many of his contemporaries had been abused and had suffered mental and physical breakdowns, and asked what support the school had offered. The review says the headmaster's reply contradicts the evidence in Bull's own personnel file and in governing body minutes, and it found no sign of any follow-up.

In 2017 another former pupil emailed the chairman of governors to say Bull had abused him when they were both pupils, and was told to go to the police. The review has not seen the reply and does not know who sent it. It found no record that the email was passed to the headmaster, the safeguarding lead or the police, which it says was by then a failure to meet statutory guidance, and it describes the response to him as dismissive. The same man told the review that another former member of staff had set up a situation in which he felt obliged to shower with Bull. In 2024 a third former pupil told the school it had never held itself accountable for the number of pupils Bull abused.

The review concludes that police held prima facie evidence against Bull in 1997 and that, on the balance of probability, a number of pupils were harmed by him both when he was a pupil and while he was a coach at the school. It found no evidence that the school pursued the matter after his death or offered support to anyone affected, and that its later responses to former pupils were inadequate and lacked empathy. It says further investigation now is unlikely to change those findings.
## Pickthall, and the school's culture

The review found no evidence that Pickthall and Bull worked together, but says the prestige both men brought, as a renowned musician and a fencing coach, may have made school leaders reluctant to believe concerns about them. Former pupils described Pickthall as godlike and bigger than the school, and one described the school of the mid-1980s to mid-1990s as having a culture of fear. Pupils told the review they did not report abuse because they feared not being believed or harming their chances in music. On Pickthall, the review found anonymous allegations in 2007, 2009 and 2014 were not properly investigated, and a misplaced personnel file meant earlier warnings were not seen.

The review also heard what it called credible accounts of abuse by other staff in the 1960s and 1970s, including harsh physical punishment, and of abuse by pupils. It says the staff named in those accounts have died or cannot be traced.
## What the school says

In a foreword, the chairman of governors, Lord Black of Brentwood, who was a pupil at the school in the 1970s and early 1980s, offers a "deep, sincere and unreserved apology" to everyone abused in the school's past. He says the governors have accepted the report and all its recommendations, and that the school has learned the lessons. Nobody, he writes, will ever again hide behind the idea that it could not happen there, because it did.

Lord Black says safeguarding is now the first item of business whenever governors meet, and that the school has changed out of all recognition since Pickthall left in 2014. He points to inspections by the Independent Schools Inspectorate in 2019, 2022 and 2025, and to two independent safeguarding reviews the school commissioned in light of Pickthall's crimes, in 2022 and 2025. The review itself agrees that safeguarding at the school today is strong, well resourced and led from the top, and that pupils describe the school as happy and safe.

On its website, the school lists 17 designated safeguarding leads and deputies. It says every senior school pupil carries a card with the names of people they can talk to and the numbers of outside organisations, and that pupils can report a concern through an online platform called The Student Voice.
## What happens next

The review makes recommendations that the school has accepted. They include publicly acknowledging the harm done by Pickthall, Bull, other adults and pupils, and accepting that the school failed to detect abuse during the 1980s, 1990s and 2000s; sharing the report with the Essex Safeguarding Children Board; sharing the findings about Bull with British Fencing and the British Olympic Committee; training staff and governors in how sex offenders groom children; and checking that no other complaints about current or former staff have been misfiled.

British Fencing said on Friday 20 November that it would commission its own independent safeguarding review into the role, if any, of the sport's governing body and its predecessor, the Amateur Fencing Association. The former pupil who wrote to the school in 2017 has asked, in his evidence to the review, whether British Fencing and the British Olympic Committee were told about Bull in 1997.

Outside the school, Bull coached at Wickford Fencing Club from 1979 to 1987, according to the club's history page, which lists him among its previous coaches. The review makes no findings about his time at the Wickford club.
## About Brentwood School

Brentwood School was founded in 1557 by Sir Antony Browne, a lawyer who later became one of England's most senior judges, and received its licence from Queen Mary on 5 July 1558. Its Tudor schoolroom, Old Big School, was built in 1568.

Today it is a private, fee-paying school and a registered charity, with more than 1,800 boys and girls aged 3 to 18 and boarding for older pupils. Boys and girls are taught together in the prep school and sixth form, but in separate classes from 11 to 16, an approach the school calls the Diamond Model.

Fees for 2026/27 are £30,204 a year for day pupils from Year 7 to the sixth form, including VAT, which has been charged on private school fees since January 2025. Full boarding costs £58,464 a year. Fees for younger pupils run from £16,500 a year for three-year-olds to £23,076 in Years 3 to 6. The school's charity had an income of £44.9 million in the year to August 2024, according to the Charity Commission.

Except where stated, everything in this story comes from the review. The 1974 result comes from published championship results, his Wickford coaching from the club's own website, details of the school's safeguarding team from its website, and British Fencing's plans from its statement on Friday. The school's history, fees and size come from its own website, the Independent Schools Council and the Independent Schools Yearbook, and its income from the Charity Commission register.
## Where to get help

Brentwood School says victim-survivors can contact the headmaster or the chairman of governors in confidence. The review lists organisations that support adults abused in childhood: NAPAC on 0808 801 0331, Stop It Now on 0808 1000 900, SERICC on 01375 380609 and CARA Essex on 01206 769795. British Fencing has a form for reporting a safeguarding concern on its website. Samaritans is available any time on 116 123.

body: The council looked at knocking down Leisure World and building a new centre, but judged that the cost and the years it would take ruled that out for now, it said on 16 November. Instead, council leaders want a programme of work on the existing site covering essential building infrastructure, customer facilities and the systems that keep the centre running.

The plans were examined by the council's Scrutiny Committee on 11 November and go to the Cabinet for a final decision on Wednesday 2 December. The council says fuller details and a timetable for the work will follow if they are approved.

Council leader Paul Dundas, Conservative councillor for Tiptree, said that like many ageing public buildings, the site "now requires major investment". A brand-new centre would have been the ideal answer, he said, but it was not viable at this stage. He said it would not be "remotely acceptable" for a city of more than 200,000 people to have no public swimming, and called the plan the biggest investment in Leisure World for a generation.

The council has not yet said what the programme will cost. Its 2026/27 budget, agreed in February, set aside £8 million to be invested in Leisure World. After the scrutiny meeting, Mr Dundas told the Daily Gazette the centre would have faced permanent closure within months without the investment.

The work would follow the £1.4 million refurbishment of the Leisure Pool, which closed at the end of September and is due to reopen in early 2027. That project covers relining the pool, new changing areas, work on the outdoor flumes, better ventilation, a new splash pad and upgraded water features. The rest of Leisure World has stayed open, though its main pool [shut for cleaning after an incident](/story/colchester-leisure-world-swimming-pool-closed-incident/) on Friday 20 November.

The decision falls during the reorganisation of Essex councils. Colchester has said that during 2026/27 it expects to share any substantial financial decisions with the other councils that will form its new unitary authority.

body: Southend-on-Sea City Council gave permission for 17 student rooms on the first, second and third floors of 6-7 Clifftown Road on 28 November 2025, and those floors have since been converted, Your Southend reports. A new application from McNamara, Brook and Mac Property Developments Ltd, registered on 16 November 2026, asks for the same 17 rooms to become a house in multiple occupation (HMO) that anyone can rent.

Days after the 2025 approval, on 2 December, the University of Essex announced it would close its Southend campus. It shut at the end of August 2026, with courses moving to Colchester. Your Southend says it is not known whether the closure led to the new plan.
## What is a shared house, or HMO?

Under the Housing Act 2004, an HMO is a home rented by at least three people who are not one family and who share a kitchen, bathroom or toilet. Each tenant normally rents their own room and shares the rest. The council's guidance counts a family, or a couple, as one household.

When five or more people from two or more households share, the HMO needs a licence from the council, and running one without a licence is a criminal offence. Shared houses for more than six people also fall outside the usual planning categories for homes, so they need full planning permission.
## What happens next

The council normally writes to neighbours and puts up a site notice, and anyone can comment on the plans on its planning website using reference 26/01422/FUL. Planning officers usually decide applications like this themselves, but a councillor can ask for one to go to the council's Development Control Committee, as happened with a 15-bed HMO in Cobham Road, Westcliff, in 2023.
## What the council will look at

Southend's planning rules set minimum bedroom sizes in shared homes of 6.5 square metres for one person and 10.2 square metres for two, require shared living space, and steer this kind of housing towards the city centre, where the building stands. Officers also weigh noise and privacy for neighbours, bin storage, cycle parking and transport. In the Cobham Road report, officers proposed conditions including a cap on the number of residents and a secure cycle space for every room.

The council can approve the plans, approve them with conditions or refuse them. If they are refused, the developer can appeal to the Planning Inspectorate. Until a decision is made, the existing permission means the rooms can only be let to students.
## If the plans are approved

If permission is granted, the landlord would still need an HMO licence before the rooms are let to five or more people. Licences cover fire safety, overcrowding, repairs and the kitchens and bathrooms tenants share, and the council says its private sector housing officers visit every HMO in the city. Failing to apply for a licence can bring a penalty of up to £30,000, and the council can take over the running of a property that should be licensed but is not.
## The rest of the building

The ground-floor shop and basement are not part of the plan. They are being marketed separately to businesses at £54,000 a year, Your Southend reports. Ravens, a family-run department store best known for its menswear, closed in 2017.

body: Officers seized 616kg of raw tobacco from an industrial unit in the Brentwood area during a nationwide HM Revenue and Customs operation against illegal cigarette production, HMRC has revealed.

The raids on 10 November centred on an industrial site in Bourne, Lincolnshire, where HMRC says it found a fully working cigarette factory. Officers seized 808,840 cigarettes and about 4.8 tonnes of tobacco there, along with machinery for cutting and drying tobacco and for making and packing cigarettes. HMRC's first assessment is that the plant could produce more than 200,000 cigarettes a day.

About 200 officers carried out 12 search warrants at homes and industrial premises across England. Besides the Brentwood unit, they searched industrial premises in Grantham, Kirkby-in-Ashfield and Northampton. From homes in Willenhall, Greenwich and Newham they took £645,000 in cash and four gold bars worth about £213,500. In all, more than 1.4 million cigarettes and about 5.5 tonnes of tobacco were seized, carrying an estimated £4.5m in duty.

Twenty-one people were arrested on suspicion of offences linked to the fraudulent evasion of excise duty. All have been released pending further enquiries. HMRC has not said where in the Brentwood area the unit is. The operation was led by HMRC's Fraud Investigation Service, supported by police, the East Midlands Special Operations Unit and the Home Office.

Raw tobacco is the unprocessed leaf that cigarettes are made from. Since April 2017 anyone in the UK who holds, moves or uses it has needed HMRC's approval under the Raw Tobacco Approval Scheme, which was brought in to stop leaf being diverted into illegal cigarette making.

Margaret Mousley, deputy director of HMRC's Fraud Investigation Service, said: "This was a major operation which dismantled a huge cigarette factory, disrupting the organised criminality that sits behind it. Our investigation into that criminality is ongoing." HMRC is asking anyone with information about the illegal manufacture or sale of tobacco to report it online.

body: Labelling is not a matter for the district council. In Essex it falls to the county council's trading standards service, which has looked at how Maldon Salt is made before, as [our story last Sunday on the Observer's findings](/story/maldon-salt-german-rock-salt-sea-salt-observer/) set out.
## What trading standards found in 2019

Trading standards officers visited the firm's works at Longwick Farm, near Goldhanger, with the Food Standards Agency on 6 November 2019 and took samples. After advice from a public analyst, the FSA and Defra, they decided no further action was needed. Maldon Salt says the FSA and trading standards are satisfied with how its product is described and know exactly how the rock salt is used.

A county council trading standards spokesperson told the Observer there were no specific legal rules for deciding whether a product can accurately be described as sea salt. The UK has no legal definition of sea salt, and The Grocer, the food industry's trade magazine, says that means Maldon is doing nothing wrong under current UK labelling law.
## A stricter rule in Canada

Other countries draw the line more clearly. Canada's food inspection agency says sea salt means salt processed from an existing sea, and salt from a mine cannot be labelled that way. In Canada, Maldon's packs are labelled Maldon Salt and list the ingredient as salt flakes. The Observer reported that the firm had not commented on the change.
## What the Observer found

As [The Seax reported last Sunday](/story/maldon-salt-german-rock-salt-sea-salt-observer/), an Observer investigation found that Maldon Salt mixes rock salt mined in Germany by K+S into the seawater it draws from the Blackwater estuary, and estimated that about 50 tonnes arrive each week. The paper reported that the firm bought its rock salt from Cheshire until about 2020 and has mostly bought it from Germany since.

Maldon Salt does not dispute that some of the added rock salt ends up in the finished flakes. It says rock salt is ancient sea salt from prehistoric seas, that its "100% sea salt flakes" label is accurate, that it has never hidden its salt-on-salt method, and that its products comply with food and labelling law in every market where they are sold.
## The planning history

Deliveries of salt to Longwick Farm have a long planning history. The Observer reported that the 2006 permission for the works covered salt made from Blackwater water, that a condition added in 2011 banned salt being delivered to the site for making or selling salt, and that the firm applied to lift it the following year, was refused by the council and won on appeal. Neighbours have questioned the deliveries since they first filmed them in 2010.
Maldon Salt has made salt in the town for 144 years and is a major local employer. No UK regulator has taken action against it over the way its salt is made or labelled.

body: She followed her older brother, Kevin, into Essex Police. The force describes her as a self-confessed maverick with a sharp sense of humour and a dedication to high standards, and calls her retirement the end of an era.

Her early years were eventful. One of her first jobs for CID involved having to drink in a student bar, and in her first year she was sent flying through the window of a shop in Colchester after being hit by a car.

A newspaper cutting from her recruit days, shared by the force, shows her in the front row of a new intake under the headline "Almost half recruit squad are women". It names her as the most successful recruit at training school and says she was posted to Colchester.

Later in her career she became an innovator. Her work on HOLMES, the computer system police use to manage information during major investigations, and on the National Police Chiefs' Council's Casualty Bureau saw her ideas adopted across the country.
She is a former winner of the force's Liam Brigginshaw Award for outstanding commitment, which she received in 2024.
Essex Police shared the news of her retirement on its Facebook page on Saturday morning, and says more about her career is on its website.
